pages.title: DiagramStack
pages.summary: The illustrator/canvas stack: how a diagram goes from text to a drawing on a canvas, and which package owns each step.
pages.content:
The illustrator/canvas stack: how a diagram goes from text to a drawing on a canvas, and which package owns each step. `@dxos/diagram` is the headless core: the scene model, the `.dx` DSL, its layout engines and the layout checks. `plugin-illustrator` binds that core to the `Drawing` ECHO type and to the agent operations. The renderer variants (`plugin-canvas`, `plugin-tldraw`, `plugin-excalidraw`, and the plugin's own SVG variant) store a scene in their own record format. The consumers draw through the operations or call the core directly.

This document covers the stack as a whole and the diagram kinds of the DSL. Each package keeps its own spec for what is inside it: [plugin-illustrator](https://github.com/dxos/dxos/blob/main/packages/plugins/plugin-illustrator/PLUGIN.mdl) for the operations and the variant seam, [react-ui-canvas](https://github.com/dxos/dxos/blob/main/packages/ui/react-ui-canvas/SPEC.mdl) for the scene engine behind `plugin-canvas`, and [DIAGRAM.mdl](https://github.com/dxos/dxos/blob/main/packages/common/diagram/rules/DIAGRAM.mdl) for the appeal rules that score a layout.

## Stack

Each arrow points at a package the source package depends on (its `package.json` `dependencies`). Plugin names drop their `plugin-` prefix. The `diagram` blocks in this document are the sources; regenerate a render with `moon run plugin-illustrator:render-diagrams -- <abs path>/spec/diagrams/<name>.dx`.

![@dxos/diagram is the base. plugin-illustrator and react-ui-canvas depend on it; the variants canvas, tldraw and excalidraw depend on plugin-illustrator, and canvas also on react-ui-canvas; the consumers uml and drawing-app depend on canvas, dx drawing on plugin-illustrator, @dxos/drawing and plugin-code on @dxos/diagram.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dxos/dxos/main/packages/common/diagram/spec/diagrams/stack.dx.svg)

```diagram
diagram
node Diagram "@dxos/diagram" ref="packages/common/diagram"
node Illustrator "illustrator" ref="packages/plugins/plugin-illustrator"
group variants "Renderer variants" {
  node ReactCanvas "react-ui-canvas" ref="packages/ui/react-ui-canvas"
  node Canvas "canvas" ref="packages/plugins/plugin-canvas"
  node Tldraw "tldraw" ref="packages/plugins/plugin-tldraw"
  node Excalidraw "excalidraw" ref="packages/plugins/plugin-excalidraw"
}
group consumers "Consumers" {
  node Uml "uml" ref="packages/plugins/plugin-uml"
  node App "drawing-app" ref="packages/apps/drawing-app"
  node Cli "dx drawing" ref="packages/devtools/cli"
  node DrawingCli "@dxos/drawing" ref="packages/devtools/drawing"
  node Code "code" ref="packages/plugins/plugin-code"
}
edge Illustrator -> Diagram
edge ReactCanvas -> Diagram
edge Canvas -> Illustrator
edge Canvas -> ReactCanvas
edge Tldraw -> Illustrator
edge Excalidraw -> Illustrator
edge Uml -> Canvas
edge App -> Canvas
edge Cli -> Illustrator
edge DrawingCli -> Diagram
edge Code -> Diagram
```

## Pipeline

A diagram is text until a variant stores it. `Dsl.read` parses the text and collects the semantic statements into a `Semantic.Diagram`. The engine for its kind lays it out as `Scene.Command[]`, and the variant's builder writes those as records into the drawing's canvas. `Diagnostics` reads the scene back and reports what is wrong with the layout, which is what lets an agent fix its own drawing. The figure is itself a data-flow diagram ([F-3]).

![The author's .dx source flows to Dsl.read, a Semantic.Diagram to the engine for its kind, Scene.Command[] to the variant builder, records into the Drawing.Canvas store, the scene to Diagnostics, and the report back to the author.](spec/diagrams/pipeline.dx.svg)

```diagram
diagram kind=dataflow
node Author "Author or agent" role=external
node Read "Dsl.read" ref="packages/common/diagram/src/dsl/parse.ts"
node Layout "Engine by kind" ref="packages/common/diagram/src/dsl/compile.ts"
node Apply "Variant builder" ref="packages/common/diagram/src/content.ts"
node Store "Drawing.Canvas" role=store ref="packages/plugins/plugin-illustrator/src/types/Drawing.ts"
node Check "Diagnostics" ref="packages/common/diagram/src/diagnostics.ts"
edge Author -> Read ".dx source"
edge Read -> Layout "Semantic.Diagram"
edge Layout -> Apply "Scene.Command[]"
edge Apply -> Store "records"
edge Store -> Check "scene"
edge Check -> Author "report"
```

## Types

The headless model, in `src/scene.ts` and `src/semantic.ts`. None of it depends on ECHO or React.

- **type** `Scene` A drawing as renderer-neutral data: named world objects, each a list of elements in object-local units.

- **type** `WorldObject` One thing the drawing depicts ("server", a participant, a group frame), placed by `origin` and `scale`.

- **type** `Element` A graphical primitive inside an object: rect, ellipse, diamond, triangle, circle, line, curve, arc, text, arrow, portal.

- **type** `Command` An edit to a scene: upsert-object, upsert-elements, remove-elements, remove-object, move-object.

- **type** `Diagram` The semantic statements of a document, before any coordinate exists (`Semantic.Diagram`).

- **type** `DiagramKind` What a diagram depicts, which decides its layout ([F-1]).

- **type** `Step` One entry of a sequence timeline, in source order; a fragment holds sections of steps.

## Components

- **component** `Dsl` The `.dx` language (`src/dsl/`): a Lezer grammar, `read` (text to commands plus a semantic diagram), `parse` (laid out synchronously, for an editor), `compile` (the full search), `print` (canonical text of a scene) and…

- **component** `SemanticEngine` Lays out `structure` and `dataflow` diagrams: a scored grid search places the boxes, a channel router draws the connectors through the gutters, and the layout objective picks among the routed candidates.

- **component** `SequenceEngine` Lays out `sequence` diagrams (`src/sequence-engine.ts`).

- **component** `Dataflow` The data-flow roles (`src/dataflow.ts`): the shapes for process, store and external, and the rule checks over the flows.

- **component** `Diagnostics` Analyzes any scene, whatever made it: overlaps, connectors through nodes and labels that do not fit are errors, crossings and bends are warnings, plus the metrics the objective scores.

- **component** `ContentHandler` The seam to a renderer (`src/content.ts`): maps a scene object onto the renderer's records and reads the scene back from them.

- **component** `MermaidDialects` DEPRECATED.

## Features

- **feat** `F-1` Diagram kinds
  - `F-1.1` `diagram kind=` selects the engine: `structure` (the default), `sequence` or `dataflow`.
  - `F-1.2` A statement or word that belongs to one kind is an error in the others: `note`, `fragment`, `calls`, `sends` and `returns` outside a sequence diagram, `role=actor` outside a sequence diagram, `role=process|store|externa…
  - `F-1.3` `note`, `fragment` and `else` are contextual keywords.
  - `F-1.4` `Dsl.parse` and `Dsl.compile` give the same result for a sequence diagram; neither searches.

- **feat** `F-2` Sequence diagrams
  - `F-2.1` Participants are the nodes, in declaration order from left to right; the members of a `group` stay adjacent and are framed together.
  - `F-2.2` Messages are the edges, one row each, top to bottom in source order.
  - `F-2.3` `->` is a plain message, `calls` a synchronous call, `sends` an asynchronous message (open head), `returns` a reply (dashed, open head).
  - `F-2.4` a `calls` message reaches its target → an activation bar opens on the target and closes at the `returns` that answers it; a nested call stacks a bar offset beside the first
  - `F-2.5` A bar that no `returns` closes ends with the fragment section it opened in, or else after the last message its participant takes part in.
  - `F-2.6` A `returns` with no open call, or to a participant other than the innermost caller, is drawn and reported as a warning.
  - `F-2.7` `note A "…"` sits right of A, `note A:left "…"` left of it, `note A, B "…"` spans both.
  - `F-2.8` `fragment alt|opt|loop|par|break|critical ["guard"] { … }` frames its steps with an operator tab and a guard; `alt` and `par` take further sections with `else ["guard"] { … }`, divided by a dashed line; fragments nest.
  - `F-2.9` The space between two lifelines grows to fit the widest label, message to self or note between them, so no label overlaps a lifeline it does not belong to.
  - `F-2.10` Pins, placement relations, sides, waypoints, buses and relationship words are ignored in a sequence diagram, each with a warning on its own statement.
  - `F-2.11` `role=actor` draws a participant as a stick figure with its name under it.
  - `F-2.12` A laid-out sequence diagram has no `Diagnostics` errors and no crossings: lifelines, dividers and group frames are guide lines.

- **feat** `F-3` Data-flow diagrams
  - `F-3.1` Each node has a role: `process` (the default) is drawn as a bubble, `store` as a square box with its id (`D1`, `D2`, … in declaration order) in a compartment on the left, `external` as a shaded square box.
  - `F-3.2` Placement, routing, groups and hints work as in a structure diagram.
  - `F-3.3` A flow whose ends are both non-processes (external or store) is reported as a warning: data moves only through a process.
  - `F-3.4` A process with inputs and no outputs (a black hole), a process with outputs and no inputs (a miracle), and a store that is written and never read are reported as warnings.

- **feat** `F-4` Mermaid is deprecated
  - `F-4.1` The `generate` operation and the mermaid compilers are marked deprecated and keep working.
  - `F-4.2` The agent skills teach the `.dx` DSL and do not ask for mermaid.
  - `F-4.3` `Dsl.convert` stays, as the way an existing mermaid source becomes DSL text.
  - `F-4.4` Neither `Dsl.compile` nor `draw` needs mermaid input.

## The `draw` call

What happens when an agent calls `draw`. The figure is itself a sequence diagram ([F-2]).

![The agent calls the Draw op with a source; the op calls Dsl.compile, which calls SequenceEngine.solve for kind=sequence and SemanticEngine.compile otherwise; if there are no errors the op applies the commands through the variant builder; it then has Diagnostics analyze the scene and returns the scene and report to the agent.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dxos/dxos/main/packages/common/diagram/spec/diagrams/draw.dx.svg)

```diagram
diagram kind=sequence
node Agent "Agent" role=actor
node Op "Draw op" ref="packages/plugins/plugin-illustrator/src/operations/draw.ts"
node Dsl "Dsl.compile" ref="packages/common/diagram/src/dsl/compile.ts"
node Engine "Layout engine" ref="packages/common/diagram/src/sequence-engine.ts"
node Variant "Variant builder" ref="packages/plugins/plugin-illustrator/src/types/IllustratorCapabilities.ts"
node Diag "Diagnostics" ref="packages/common/diagram/src/diagnostics.ts"
edge Agent calls Op "draw(source)"
edge Op calls Dsl "compile"
fragment alt "kind=sequence" {
  edge Dsl calls Engine "SequenceEngine.solve"
  edge Engine returns Dsl "commands"
} else "structure, dataflow" {
  edge Dsl calls Engine "SemanticEngine.compile"
  edge Engine returns Dsl "commands, issues"
}
edge Dsl returns Op "commands, problems"
fragment opt "no errors" {
  edge Op calls Variant "apply(commands)"
  edge Variant returns Op "upserted"
}
edge Op calls Diag "analyze(scene)"
edge Diag returns Op "diagnostics"
edge Op returns Agent "scene, report"
```

## Acceptance

- **scenario** `T-1` A sequence diagram lays out cleanly

- **scenario** `T-2` An activation spans its call and return

- **scenario** `T-3` Data-flow roles and rules

- **scenario** `T-4` The skill examples draw

## Open questions

- The DSL cannot show class members (attributes, methods) in a box, which is the one thing only mermaid's classDiagram still does. Until it can, mermaid cannot be removed.
- The layout engine's eval corpus (`plugin-illustrator/docs/diagrams/*.mmd`) is mermaid. Moving it to `.dx` changes the corpus snapshots, so it is a change of its own.
- tldraw and excalidraw records have nowhere to keep `guide`; a sequence diagram replayed onto them reads its lifelines back as plain lines.

pages.title: Deus
pages.summary: The spec for `@dxos/deus` itself: the tooling around the `.mdl` language.
pages.content:
The spec for `@dxos/deus` itself: the tooling around the `.mdl` language. The language is defined in `lang/` and motivated in `docs/DESIGN.md`. This document covers what the package must do, so far only for the spec changelog.

## Features

- **feat** `F-1` Attributed decision log
  - `F-1.1` Each decision names exactly one decider in `by:`, typed `user:<handle>` (GitHub username or email) or `agent:<name>`.
  - `F-1.2` An agent is named by its harness, never by the model that served it.
  - `F-1.3` An `agent:` decision names the person it acted for in `for:`; a `user:` decision has no `for:`.
  - `F-1.4` A `user:` decision restates what the person said: references resolved, context included and wording fixed, with no information added or removed.
  - `F-1.5` The log is append-only.
  - `F-1.6` Decision ids are `D-1`, `D-2`, … in the order appended, newest last.
  - `F-1.7` Approval of agent decisions is a new `user:` decision whose prose says what it approves.
  - `F-1.8` A decision records a choice about the specified system.

- **feat** `F-2` Every spec change adds a decision
  - `F-2.1` A change to a spec outside `## Changelog` adds at least one new decision.
  - `F-2.2` A new spec starts with at least one decision.
  - `F-2.3` `deus changelog check` enforces F-1.5, F-1.6, F-2.1 and F-2.2 by comparing each changed `.mdl` file with the merge base, and runs in CI as "Check spec changelogs".
  - `F-2.4` Language definitions (`lang/`), review rules (`rules/`) and test fixtures are not specs and are exempt.
  - `F-2.5` Only `decision` blocks under `## Changelog` form the log; examples elsewhere are ignored.
  - `F-2.6` A trivial edit needs no decision: whitespace, or at most 3 words each fixed by an edit distance of at most a third of the word, where no changed word has a digit or is a normative word.
  - `F-2.7` A `Spec-Changelog-Skip: <reason>` trailer on any branch commit waives F-2.1 for that branch; the append-only rules still apply.
  - `F-2.8` A change with no spec decision behind it, such as adding a diagram or reorganizing sections, carries the F-2.7 trailer instead of a process decision.

- **feat** `F-3` Linting
  - `F-3.1` The editor linter and `deus lint` report decisions that break F-1.1 or F-1.3.
  - `F-3.2` `deus lint --only <source>` restricts output to one check, so the block-type check (which knows only built-in types) does not hide decision errors.
  - `F-3.3` `.agents/skills/mdl/scripts/check-decisions.ts` asks TypeSafe System One whether each decision a branch adds breaks F-1.8, giving it the spec's name and introduction so a spec whose system is itself a process is judged…

- **feat** `F-4` Agent guidance
  - `F-4.1` The repo has an `mdl` skill (`.agents/skills/mdl/SKILL.md`) for writing specs and recording decisions.
  - `F-4.2` The skill tells an agent to record a person's input first, faithfully — adding context, never assumptions — and its own additions as separate decisions.
  - `F-4.3` The skill tells an agent where to read the person's handle from the environment, so it never asks or guesses.
  - `F-4.4` The skill tells an agent to leave process out of the changelog (F-1.8), including a person's process instructions, and to run `check-decisions.ts` before committing.

- **feat** `F-5` Command-line interface
  - `F-5.1` `@dxos/deus` ships one `deus` CLI, built with Effect CLI, and every `.mdl` tool in the repo that belongs to Deus is a subcommand of it: `changelog check`, `lint`, `qa list`, `qa lint` and `review items|check`.
  - `F-5.2` The command tree is exported from `@dxos/deus/cli`, and the `dx` CLI mounts it as `dx deus`.
  - `F-5.3` `pnpm deus` runs the CLI from source with plain `node` at the repo root, so CI and agents need no build.
  - `F-5.4` `qa list` prints the numbered `test` and `suite` blocks that `/dxos:qa` addresses; `qa lint` reports references a test never binds and teardowns that could remove an object the run did not create.
  - `F-5.5` `review items` lists every item a spec review must judge; `review check` validates a `.review.mdl` against its spec and the checkout.

- **feat** `F-6` SQL tables
  - `F-6.1` The `table` block (`lang/sql.mdl`, `org.dxos.mdl.table@1.0`) declares a SQL table a component owns: its columns with SQLite storage classes and SQL constraints, its keys and indexes, and the migration set it lives in.
  - `F-6.2` A `table` states the schema after the spec's changes; `new:` marks the table or the columns the spec adds.
  - `F-6.3` A `table` is a spec item that requirements cite as `table:<name>` or `table:<name>.<column>`, and `deus lint` knows the block type.
  - `F-6.4` A spec refers to code by component or symbol name and to another spec by its frontmatter `id`, never by file path; a `table` names its store and migration-history table, not a migrations directory.
  - `F-6.5` A `table` is part of the spec's data model: the viewer's Data model view shows it as a stored root with its columns as fields, its store as a tag, and a `REFERENCES <table>(<column>)` column as a reference to that table.

- **feat** `F-7` Showcases
  - `F-7.1` The `showcase` block (`lang/showcase.mdl`, `org.dxos.mdl.showcase@1.0`) links features of a spec to a recorded example of them: the presentation a pull request produced when it implemented them.
  - `F-7.2` A showcase is non-normative; it is not a spec item, and a spec review does not judge it.
  - `F-7.3` A `showcase` names the `feat` and `req` ids it shows in `for:`, and `deus lint` reports one that names none or names an id the document does not declare.
  - `F-7.4` A showcase carries its pull request and media as URLs, never a file path; its deck is located from its id.

pages.title: WorkerFramework
pages.summary: Generic worker management framework for DXOS client services.
pages.content:
Generic worker management framework for DXOS client services. It elects a single leader tab that hosts a dedicated worker, connects follower tabs to that worker via a coordinator that exchanges `MessagePort`s, and survives leader death through lock stealing, re-election, and reconnection. RPC over the worker boundary is effect-native (`@effect/rpc`).

This spec captures the package's namespace modules and their public API, plus the framework's features and acceptance criteria.

Modules follow the DXOS namespace-module styleguide: PascalCase file in `src/`, marked `// @import-as-namespace`, re-exported from an `index.ts` as `export * as <Name> from './<Name>'`, and consumed by callers as a namespace (`RpcTiming.serverLayer`, never a bare `rpcTimingServerLayer`). Members are unprefixed — the caller always reads `<Name>.<member>`. The subpath entrypoints (`client`, `worker`, `coordinator`) are each consumed as a namespace of the subpath (`import * as Client from '@dxos/worker-framework/client'`).

## Modules

### `@dxos/worker-framework` (root)

The generic effect-rpc-over-`MessagePort` composition (client/serve helpers) is intentionally NOT part of this package. It lives as the `Rpc` namespace in `@dxos/client-protocol`, keeping worker-framework to transport plumbing (ports, leader election, coordinator, protocol). A minimal internal copy under `src/internal/rpc.ts` backs only the package's own stories and the RpcTiming test.

- **module** `RpcTiming` Effect RPC middleware that measures per-request queue-wait and service time across the worker boundary.

`RpcTiming` lives in `src/RpcTiming.ts`. The `Metadata` and `Middleware` Effect tags retain the stable global identifiers `'RpcTimingMetadata'` / `'RpcTimingMiddleware'`; only their exported member names are unprefixed.

### `@dxos/worker-framework/client`

- **module** `Client` The follower/leader tab connection.

### `@dxos/worker-framework/worker`

- **module** `Worker` The dedicated-worker runtime loop: storage lock, liveness lock, displacement of prior workers, and the init/ready/session protocol with owner detection.

### `@dxos/worker-framework/coordinator`

- **module** `Coordinator` Cross-tab message routing between followers and the leader.

### Shared protocol types

- **module** `WorkerProtocol` The wire protocol shared across the Client, Worker, and Coordinator modules, plus the error codec it posts; re-exported from every entrypoint that references them.

## Features

- **feat** `F-1` Leader election
  - `F-1.1` a tab opens a Client.Connection → it requests the LEADER Web Lock; the tab that acquires it is
  - `F-1.2` a tab holds the leader lock → it broadcasts a `leader-heartbeat` every `heartbeatInterval` (default 1s)
  - `F-1.3` a follower observes no heartbeat for `staleTimeout` (default 5s) and the → it may steal the lock to force re-election, subject to a steal cooldown
  - `F-1.4` a leader session fails (worker init/crash) rather than the lock being stolen → the tab re-enters election after a capped exponential backoff with jitter,
  - `F-1.5` the worker replies `init-failed` while the tab has not yet connected → open() rejects with the worker's decoded error, whatever its name, and the
  - `F-1.6` a tab's own port request times out while it holds the leader lock, or its → it never steals — its own lock, or a healthy leader it merely cannot hear —
  - `F-1.7` the leader lock is stolen, or the connection closes, while the leader session is → the session is closed once it finishes opening and its worker terminated, so the
  - `F-1.8` `maxLeaderFailures` consecutive leader-session or connect-handle failures occur → open() rejects with that failure at once instead of at the end of its budget, and

- **feat** `F-2` Session and port exchange
  - `F-2.1` a follower needs a worker session → it sends `request-port`; the leader asks the worker to `start-session`;
  - `F-2.2` a follower sees a `new-leader` or `leader-heartbeat` before it has a port → it re-sends `request-port`, recovering from a missed one-shot `new-leader`
  - `F-2.3` the worker receives repeated `start-session` for the same clientId → it de-duplicates and serves a single session per client
  - `F-2.4` a `provide-port` arrives carrying an `attempt` other than the tab's current one → it is ignored — the worker closes that session when it serves the current attempt
  - `F-2.5` the worker cannot build a session whose ports it already handed out → it posts `session-failed`; the leader relays it; the tab fails that attempt with

- **feat** `F-3` Worker lifecycle and displacement
  - `F-3.1` a worker starts → it holds the `storageLockKey` Web Lock for its whole lifetime and
  - `F-3.2` a worker becomes ready → it holds a per-instance liveness Web Lock before advertising `ready`, and
  - `F-3.3` the leader sends `init` with config and an `ownerClientId` → the worker builds its runtime, marks the owning client, and replies `ready`
  - `F-3.4` building the runtime fails → the worker replies `init-failed` with the encoded error instead of `ready`,
  - `F-3.5` a starting worker is still queued on the storage lock after its displacement → it escalates once on the same channel with a `terminate` action naming itself,
  - `F-3.6` a tab receives an escalation over the displacement channel → it discards a malformed message, ignores one its own worker raised, and otherwise
  - `F-3.7` a worker is asked `ping` → it replies `pong` with the same nonce from its message loop, which is what tells
  - `F-3.8` a tab terminates a worker that ignored displacement → it reports a `WorkerTerminationError` at error level, so the forced kill reaches
  - `F-3.9` the wedged worker's handle exposes no `terminate()` (a bare `MessagePort`, whose → the tab reports a `WorkerNotTerminableError` at error level and leaves the session
  - `F-3.10` the worker's storage or liveness lock is stolen, or `Options.signal` aborts → the worker shuts down (a pending storage-lock request is simply dropped)
  - `F-3.11` a `start-session` arrives while the worker is shutting down → it is ignored rather than forked from the closing runtime scope

- **feat** `F-4` Reconnection
  - `F-4.1` the connected worker/leader terminates (liveness lock released or a new → the follower closes the stale handle, reschedules the connect task, and
  - `F-4.2` a reconnection (not the initial connection) succeeds → all `onReconnect` callbacks run and the `reconnected` event fires; a callback
  - `F-4.3` the connection is lost while a handle is installed → the stale handle is closed (bounded) BEFORE the next connect attempt starts, and
  - `F-4.4` a connect attempt received a port but its handle failed to open → the retry waits an exponential, capped, jittered backoff; `maxLeaderFailures`

- **feat** `F-5` RPC transport

pages.title: CodeIndex
pages.summary: `code-index` indexes a repository into two databases that live side by side in one directory: a SQLite ledger of indexed files and a persistent RDF quad store holding one named graph per file.
pages.content:
`code-index` indexes a repository into two databases that live side by side in one directory: a SQLite ledger of indexed files and a persistent RDF quad store holding one named graph per file. The graph speaks the DEUS code vocabulary defined in [`design/ONTOLOGY.md`](https://github.com/dxos/dxos/blob/main/tools/code-index/design/ONTOLOGY.md) — that document is the source of truth, and the indexer emits JSON-LD shaped by it. Queries are SPARQL or typed LDkit lenses; derived relations (transitive dependencies, layering rules) are N3 rules evaluated by a rule engine rather than code. The quad store and the rule engine are one Rust Node-API addon, `tools/code-index-native` ([`design/NATIVE-BACKEND.md`](https://github.com/dxos/dxos/blob/main/tools/code-index/design/NATIVE-BACKEND.md)).

Parsing runs off the main thread: a pool of workers, addressed over Effect RPC, parses with `oxc` and resolves imports with `oxc-resolver`. Workers never touch a database, so nothing contends on SQLite or RocksDB; only the main thread writes.

The CLI is `effect/cli` on Bun. The library is Effect-native and runs on Node as well, which is where the test suite exercises it.

## Stack

| Concern            | Choice                                  | Why |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------------|-----|
| Relational store   | `@effect/sql-sqlite-{bun,node}`         | Effect-native SQL; the driver is chosen from the ambient runtime because neither loads under the other. |
| Schema             | `@dxos/sql-sqlite` `SqlMigrations` + `effect` `Migrator` | Same numbered-`.sql` migration pattern as the rest of the repo, with its own history table. |
| Quad store         | oxigraph over RocksDB (`tools/code-index-native`) | A real persistent RDF store with named graphs — deliberately not a triple table hand-rolled on SQLite. |
| SPARQL             | oxigraph                                | Evaluated in the addon off the event loop, with the default graph as the union of all file graphs; cancellable at every quad read. |
| Typed graph access | `ldkit`                                 | Schema-typed reads over the same engine, so a lens and a raw SPARQL query see one graph. |
| Reasoning          | the addon's N3 engine                   | Semi-naive evaluation of the N3 subset `rules/*.n3` uses, maintained incrementally (DRed) from the facts that changed; each rule file's conclusions land in one replaceable graph. Reachability is left to SPARQL property paths. |
| Parsing            | `oxc-parser`, `oxc-resolver`            | Real module records and real resolution, not regex. |
| Manifests          | `yaml`, `JSON.parse`                    | `moon.yml` layers and `package.json` identity, entries and workspace deps. |
| Concurrency        | `effect/rpc` over worker threads | Batches of paths in, N-Triples documents out. |
| CLI                | `effect/cli`, `@effect/platform-bun` | Subcommands, flags and help from the same Effect runtime as the library. |

## Layout

A store is one directory. It defaults to `<git root>/node_modules/.code-index` for the repository containing the working directory, so any command run anywhere inside the repo finds the same index:

```
<store>/
  index.sqlite   # file ledger + migration history + key/value meta
  native/        # the addon's RocksDB stores: oxigraph/ (quads) and journal/ (reasoning state)
```

## Indexing pass

1. **Crawl** — `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard` under the root, filtered by extension, plus each file's mtime. Git owns the ignore rules, so the index and the repository never disagree about what a file is.
2. **Diff** — compare against `files.mtime` in the ledger. Unchanged files are skipped entirely; files gone from the working tree have their graph and row removed.
3. **Dispatch** — changed paths are batched (64 by default) and sent to the worker pool.
4. **Analyze** (worker) — an analyzer chosen by filename reads the file, builds its JSON-LD document and returns it encoded as N-Triples, plus the mtime actually read: TypeScript (declarations, references, snippets), `package.json` (the `Package` node), `moon.yml` (its layer), `.mdl` (spec blocks).
5. **Upsert** (main thread) — one commit per 512 files, gathered from several worker batches: announce every file's new graph, swap the files' named graphs in one backend write, then advance every ledger row (see the commit protocol below).
6. **Reason** — the N3 rules run over the asserted facts and each reasoner's graph is replaced with the result. The phase is skipped only when the ledger records that this exact set of reasoners (a signature over their names and rules) already ran over the store's current write generation: a pass after `--no-reason`, or after one interrupted before reasoning, catches up even though it indexed nothing. With the rule set unchanged, each rule file's graph is maintained from the facts that changed since the last pass rather than recomputed.

Each phase is timed and reported (`scan`, `parse`, `commit`, `reason`, `total`); `parse` and `commit` are summed across concurrent batches, so they overlap and can exceed the wall-clock total.

## Commit safety across two stores

The two databases cannot share a transaction, so the ledger is made the single commit marker and the graph write is made idempotent:

1. `files.pending_graph` is set to the new graph IRI (`graph:file/<path>#<mtime>`) — the announcement.
2. The old graph's quads and the new graph's quads are swapped in **one** RocksDB transaction.
3. The row is updated: `graph` becomes the new IRI and `pending_graph` is cleared — the commit.

An indexing pass commits a worker batch at a time: step 1 for every file of the batch in one SQLite transaction, the per-file swaps, then step 3 for every file in another. SQLite runs in WAL mode with `synchronous=NORMAL`, which survives a process crash at any point; an OS crash can lose the last commits, but the quad store never fsyncs its own writes, so the graphs were never durable against one either.

A crash before step 3 leaves the previous revision live and the new graph reachable only through `pending_graph`; `reconcile` (run whenever the store opens) deletes exactly those graphs. Because the graph IRI carries the mtime, a half-written revision can never be mistaken for the live one. Deletion runs the other way — row first, then graph — since a graph without a row is collectable garbage while a row without a graph would be a phantom file.

## Modules

- **module** `Store` The entire persistence surface.

- **module** `Ontology` The executable mirror of `design/ONTOLOGY.md`: IRIs, the JSON-LD context the indexer emits, the document schema, and the LDkit schemas that read it back.

- **module** `Crawler` Repository discovery — git root, store location, and the non-ignored files with mtimes.

- **module** `Indexer` The main thread's half: crawl, diff against the ledger, dispatch batches to the worker pool, upsert the documents that come back.

- **module** `worker/Protocol` The RPC contract between the main thread and the parsing workers.

- **module** `worker/Pool` The worker pool client.

- **module** `worker/analyze` Dispatch: one analyzer per filename, each emitting the complete document for one file.

- **module** `worker/analyzers/typescript` Declarations and what can be seen of them structurally: what they extend, what call constructs them, what they reference and from which position, and a definition snippet.

- **module** `worker/types` Per-file type propagation inside the parse step — `design/TYPES.md`.

- **module** `worker/analyzers/package` The two files that assert a `Package` node, each from its own graph.

- **module** `worker/analyzers/spec` `.mdl` documents — frontmatter, Extensions table, and one `SpecBlock` per block with its field tree; linking them to code is a reasoner's job.

- **module** `Mdl` Reader for the `.mdl` document format: frontmatter, fenced blocks, `<type> [id][: title]` headers and indented fields.

- **module** `Cli` Subcommands and flags; the Bun entry point is `bin/code-index.ts`.

- **module** `mcp/Server` `code-index mcp`: effect's `McpServer` over stdio with one toolkit of read-only tools over a store opened with `{ readOnly: true }`.

- **module** `mcp/Sparql` Preprocessing for model-written SPARQL, shared by the MCP server and the design query explorer: missing prefixes are declared, unknown `deus:` terms are named, and a SELECT is capped at the engine.

## Commands

| Command                                | Effect |
|----------------------------------------|--------|
| `index [--root R] [--force] [--workers N] [--rules F] [--no-reason]` | Incremental pass, closed by a reasoning phase. |
| `files [--lang L]`                     | List indexed files. |
| `query <sparql> [--file]`              | SPARQL SELECT. |
| `ask <sparql> [--file]`                | SPARQL ASK. |
| `dump`                                 | Serialize the graph to N3. |
| `stats`                                | File and quad counts. |
| `clear`                                | Empty both databases. |
| `ontology`                             | Print the JSON-LD context. |
| `types [files…] [--sample N] [--seed S] [--show V]` | Score the type propagator against `tsc`. |
| `mcp`                                  | Serve the index read-only over MCP on stdio. |

`--root` defaults to the git root of the working directory, `--store` to `<root>/node_modules/.code-index`, and `--json` applies to every command.

## Features

- **feat** `F-1` One directory, two databases — A store is initialized from a directory path; `index.sqlite` (migrated) and `native/` are created inside it.
  - `F-1.1` The SQLite schema is created by numbered migrations recorded in `code_index_migrations`.
  - `F-1.2` Records and quads written in one process are visible after reopening the store.
  - `F-1.3` No module outside `Store` opens a database.
  - `F-1.4` A store recorded under another `Ontology.VERSION` is emptied on open, and the next pass reindexes everything.
  - `F-1.5` A store stamped with another backend (the retired `js` one) or with none is emptied by a writer, which rebuilds it, and refused by a reader with a request to run `code-index index`.

- **feat** `F-2` One graph per file revision — Every file's quads live in `graph:file/<path>#<mtime>`; reindexing swaps the graph rather than accumulating revisions, and removing a file drops its graph and its row.
  - `F-2.1` After a reindex the previous graph holds no quads and the ledger names the new one.
  - `F-2.2` Derived quads live in `graph:derived/<reasoner>`, which reasoning replaces wholesale.
  - `F-2.3` An interrupted commit leaves a `pending_graph` that `reconcile` deletes on the next open.
  - `F-2.4` No file path names a derived graph — file graphs and derived graphs have disjoint prefixes.

- **feat** `F-3` Incremental by mtime — The crawl compares mtimes against the ledger; unchanged files are never read or parsed.
  - `F-3.1` A second pass over an unchanged tree indexes nothing.
  - `F-3.2` Editing one file reindexes exactly that file.
  - `F-3.3` `--force` reindexes everything regardless of mtime.
  - `F-3.4` A file deleted from the working tree is removed from both databases.
  - `F-3.5` A touch that leaves the content unchanged reindexes nothing and does not rerun the reasoners.

- **feat** `F-4` Off-thread parsing — Workers receive batches of paths and return N-Triples documents; they never open a database.
  - `F-4.1` A file that cannot be read is reported as skipped, not as a failure of the pass.
  - `F-4.2` A parse failure still produces a file node, carrying `deus:parseError`.

- **feat** `F-5` Import edges — A specifier that resolves to a file inside the repository becomes a `deus:imports` edge; a bare package, a path into `node_modules`, or anything unresolvable stays a `deus:importsModule` literal.
  - `F-5.1` Ignored files (per `.gitignore`) are never crawled or indexed.
  - `F-5.2` A specifier is recorded either as an edge or as a module reference, never both.

- **feat** `F-7` Packages and containment — `package.json` asserts a `Package` node — name, version, private, public entries from the export map, workspace dependencies — and `moon.yml` adds its layer from its own graph.
  - `F-7.1` A `Package` node survives either of its two files being reindexed alone.
  - `F-7.2` Only `workspace:` ranges become `declaresDep`; catalog and registry ranges do not.

- **feat** `F-8` Structure now, meaning later — The parser records what a declaration extends, what call constructs it, what it is piped through or derived from, and what it references — as `Member` IRIs following the specifier as written.
  - `F-8.1` A bare specifier yields both a member IRI and, if it resolves inside the repo, a symbol IRI.
  - `F-8.2` References from type positions are `apiDependsOn`, from value positions `implDependsOn`.
  - `F-8.3` Every stored snippet is valid TypeScript, or absent.
  - `F-8.4` IRIs are written as the path or specifier reads (`module:@dxos/compute/Operation#make`);
  - `F-8.5` Every call to a resolvable callee that carries a literal or a configuration object, and
  - `F-8.6` Call-site literals are bounded: 8 positions, 3 object keys deep, 16 array elements,
  - `F-8.7` A reference from a top-level statement that declares nothing (`describe(…)`) is a

- **feat** `F-10` Types without a checker — The parser names the type of each variable and function symbol from its own file, in terms of the symbols imported at the boundary plus TypeScript's structural vocabulary; rules match the terms.
  - `F-10.1` Where it answers, it agrees with `tsc` — the agreement harness has no disagreements on its fixtures.
  - `F-10.2` A position it cannot type is absent, never approximated; a reference `tsc` might narrow is unknown.
  - `F-10.3` The type step costs well under a millisecond per file.
  - `F-10.4` A function or static method typed to return `Layer<…>` is a `deus:EffectLayerFactory`, providing and requiring what its returned layer does.

- **feat** `F-9` Specs are facts — A `.mdl` document yields one `SpecBlock` per block — several per fence, `req` nested in `feat` — with its fields as a tree, its body, its line and the identifiers it mentions.
  - `F-9.1` Block ids and names come from the header; two blocks sharing a key are disambiguated in order.
  - `F-9.2` The parser never fails on a `.mdl` in the repository.
  - `F-9.3` Blocks are classified, linked to code and to each other, and checked against their `ext` schema by rules (`rules/70-specs.n3`, `rules/80-gaps.n3`).

- **feat** `F-6` Derived relations are rules, recomputed with the index — Indexing closes with a reasoning phase: each rule file runs in filename order over the asserted facts and the graphs of the files before it, and its conclusions replace `graph:derived/<file>` in one transaction — mainta…
  - `F-6.1` Reachability is a query, not a rule — `deus:imports+` walks the graph lazily, and the
  - `F-6.2` A conclusion never outlives its premises — retracting an import retracts what it entailed.
  - `F-6.3` A JS pass reads the file graphs only.
  - `F-6.4` A pass skips reasoning, leaving the derived graphs as they are, only when the same reasoners already ran over the facts the store holds now.
  - `F-6.6` A rule reads only the predicates it names; an unbound predicate reads the whole graph.
  - `F-6.5` `--no-reason` skips the phase; the derived graph is then only as fresh as the last pass that ran it.
  - `F-6.8` The `resolve-refs` pass links each reference IRI to the declaration it denotes (`deus:resolvesTo`), through barrels and aliases.
  - `F-6.9` `deus:usesDeprecated` links a symbol to each `deus:deprecated` declaration it depends on, directly or through `deus:resolvesTo`.

- **feat** `F-11` An MCP server over the index — `code-index mcp` serves the store to an MCP client over stdio.
  - `F-11.1` stdout carries only JSON-RPC; every log and banner goes to stderr.
  - `F-11.2` Opening skips migration, version reset and reconcile; a missing or stale store fails with a hint.
  - `F-11.3` A store another process holds fails at startup, naming that process, rather than hanging.
  - `F-11.4` A SELECT is capped at the engine (default 200 rows, at most 2000) and reports truncation.
  - `F-11.5` `stats` counts derived graphs with a grouped SPARQL count, never by materialising quads.
  - `F-11.6` `usages` finds every symbol that uses a declaration, through barrels, re-exports, namespaces and bare specifiers, grouped by package.
- **feat** `F-12` `serve` keeps the index current — The server holds the store, and the store admits one process, so no other command can refresh it while the server runs.
  - `F-12.1` Each directory holding an indexed file, and its ancestors, is watched on its own; a recursive watch would register every directory under `node_modules`.
  - `F-12.2` A directory created under a watched one is watched at once, so files written into it later are seen.
  - `F-12.3` A new watch is followed by one more pass, which sees a file written before the watch began.
  - `F-12.4` A failed pass is reported and the watch goes on.
